article.overview: A rover mobility demonstrator is a small or medium-sized wheeled (or otherwise locomoting) robotic platform whose main purpose is to test how a vehicle moves over lunar terrain, rather than to carry a large science suite. The term describes a class of technology demonstrations, not one standard machine. Such a payload is used to prove that wheels, suspension, drive and steering, power, navigation and communications work together in the lunar environment, and to gather data on traction and soil interaction that informs later rovers. Four examples are summarised in this article. Of these, the Japanese SORA-Q nano rover and the Indian Pragyan rover are flown examples; the NASA CADRE mini-rovers are a planned mission, and the ESA Lunar Rover Mockup is a ground testbed. A historical reference, Lunokhod 1, is also noted.
article.description: A rover mobility demonstrator combines four functions. The first is locomotion: wheels or other traction elements, drive motors, and in some designs steering and articulated suspension that allow the vehicle to cross rocks, slopes and loose regolith. The second is structure and stowage: the chassis must fold, pack or otherwise fit inside a lander or deployment mechanism, and must survive launch and landing loads. The third is power and thermal management: solar cells, batteries and heaters keep the vehicle alive through the lunar day and night cycle. The fourth is autonomy and communication: cameras, inertial sensors and software allow the rover to estimate its position and avoid hazards, while a radio link passes data to a lander or to Earth. Demonstrators differ in scale. The Japanese SORA-Q (LEV-2) weighs 228 g according to JAXA. The Indian Pragyan rover has a published mass of about 26 kg in ISRO material quoted in secondary reporting. The NASA CADRE concept uses three carry-on-sized rovers that cooperate with each other and a base station. The ESA Lunar Rover Mockup is a 120 kg ground platform used to test payloads and mobility concepts.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The principal purpose of a mobility demonstrator is to reduce the technical risk of future lunar rovers. Specific objectives reported for the examples include: demonstrating autonomous surface operation (JAXA describes SORA-Q as the world's first robot to conduct fully autonomous exploration of the lunar surface, and states that LEV-2 captured and transmitted images of the SLIM lander after landing); demonstrating cooperative multi-robot operation (JAXA reports synchronised, coordinated operation of LEV-2 with LEV-1 on the lunar surface); testing traction and terrain behaviour (JAXA states that the SORA-Q design was built to handle regolith-covered terrain, and the ESA LRM is designed to test mobility on sand-compatible wheels with articulated suspension); mapping terrain and subsurface (NASA's CADRE mission plans to use stereo cameras and a multistatic ground-penetrating radar to map the surface and subsurface in 3D); and serving as a platform for payload testing (the ESA LRM is described explicitly as a platform for mounting and testing robotic payloads, including a radar speed and traversability sensor (GINGER-TD) and a robotic arm). Applications extend beyond science to operations: a demonstrated rover can be used to inspect a lander, to support astronauts, or to explore areas that are hazardous for a fixed station. These applications are proposed uses; the sources do not show that any of them has been achieved for a rover of this class except where stated above.
article.operating_principle: A wheeled mobility demonstrator moves by turning torque from motors through its wheels. Its suspension distributes the vehicle's weight so that all wheels keep contact with uneven ground. Steering may be achieved by turning the wheels, by articulating the chassis, or both. The ESA LRM uses four-wheel drive, four-wheel steering and passive chassis articulation, with four elastic titanium traction and steering wheels. SORA-Q uses a transformable design. JAXA states that it moves on two wheels, carries two visible-range cameras with CMOS detectors and was developed with TOMY, Sony and Doshisha University; its image sensor and image processing were provided by Sony according to the JAXA release. Autonomy depends on sensing the environment and deciding how to move. Cameras and inertial sensors provide data for navigation. The CADRE rovers form a mesh network with each other and with a base station on the lander, allowing them to share information during cooperative operation. The LEV-1 relay rover in the SLIM mission communicated with ground stations and relayed LEV-2's data to Earth. Because published descriptions of each design are limited, the mechanism of each individual rover should be taken from its primary source and not generalised across the class.
article.scientific_importance: Mobility is a fundamental requirement for lunar exploration. A fixed lander can study only its immediate surroundings, whereas a rover can visit geological features, sample different terrain and carry instruments across a larger area. Demonstrating mobility technology on the Moon at low cost is important because it provides data on the actual lunar surface, which laboratory tests and Earth analogue sites cannot fully reproduce. The Japanese and Indian demonstrations are scientifically significant for a second reason: they test autonomy and multi-robot cooperation in real conditions. The SORA-Q image of the SLIM lander, produced by a payload only a few hundred grams in mass, illustrates how small mobile platforms can add observational value to a larger mission.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a rover mobility demonstrator. The examples differ in scale, mission status and purpose, and their values should not be compared directly. Only values attributed to a named source are presented; where a value is not verified it is stated as such.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples span very different scales. SORA-Q is a nano rover of approximately 78 mm diameter (JAXA). Pragyan's dimensions are inconsistent across sources and are not verified. CADRE rovers are described only as about carry-on-bag size (JPL). The ESA LRM has a 1200 x 900 mm footprint and a 1000 x 760 mm payload platform (ESA). Mobility performance depends on wheel geometry, chassis articulation and ground clearance, which are not published as comparable values across these examples.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: SORA-Q: 228 g (JAXA; 250 g in secondary coverage). Pragyan: 26 kg (ISRO brochure excerpt, not verified against primary; Wikipedia). CADRE: not publicly specified. ESA LRM: 120 kg rover, 60 kg payload (ESA). Lunokhod 1 (historical reference, secondary sources only): about 756 kg; a conflicting 840 kg figure is more likely attached to Lunokhod 2 and was not verified.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: SORA-Q: not publicly specified in the sources retrieved. Pragyan: 50 W (ISRO brochure excerpt, not verified against primary). CADRE: solar-powered; no power value published. ESA LRM: two 12 V lead-acid batteries, 103 Ah (ESA; page text ambiguous).

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar mobility demonstrator must operate in a vacuum, under strong thermal cycling and in regolith that can be fine-grained and abrasive. The published CADRE plan is built around the lunar day, with operations during the daylight period of about 14 Earth days (JPL). The SORA-Q design was specifically intended for regolith-covered terrain (JAXA). Operationally, the rover must be stowed safely, released from its carrier, and brought into a state where it can move. The SLIM lander's landing, followed by LEV-2 deployment, illustrates that deployment can occur close to touchdown (JAXA). For planned missions, the power, communications and thermal interfaces must be defined with the host lander. Those interface values are not publicly specified for the CADRE mission in the source retrieved. For ground testing, the ESA LRM was designed for sand-compatible wheels and payload testing, which reflects the importance of terrain simulation in mobility development.
article.limitations: The sources available for this article are uneven. The JAXA SORA-Q information is primary but limited, with no verified surface-operation timeline. The Pragyan mass comes from a brochure excerpt that could not be retrieved directly, and its dimensions remain inconsistent. The CADRE page provides function but not mass, power or dimensions. The ESA LRM is a ground testbed, so its performance does not demonstrate lunar operation. Mobility on the Moon depends strongly on terrain, slope, regolith cohesion and lighting. A rover that traverses successfully in one area may not do so in another. The examples here should not be taken as evidence of general traverse capability.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A rover mobility demonstrator is normally carried as a payload on a lunar lander or spacecraft. For SORA-Q, the rover was carried by JAXA's SLIM lander and deployed during landing. The CADRE rovers are planned to be carried by the IM-3 lander with a base station on the lander. The ESA LRM is a ground platform and is not transported to the Moon.
transportation_process: Integrate the rover, its stowage or transformation mechanism, and its power and data interfaces with the lander on Earth.
Launch to space on a launch vehicle, followed by transfer to the Moon.
Land, with the rover either remaining on the lander or being released during the landing sequence.
Deploy onto the surface, including any transformation or unfolding of the mechanism.
Commission cameras, sensors and communications, then begin traverse operations.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For SORA-Q, JAXA reports that LEV-1 and LEV-2 were deployed during landing, and the JAXA image set shows the rover before and after deployment. The JAXA release states that the rover transformed after deployment. Whether the rover was ejected or dropped from the lander is not stated in the sources retrieved, and this article does not assume it. For CADRE, the stowage method, release mechanism and mounting interface are not described in the sources retrieved.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: SORA-Q (JAXA SLIM, January 2024) deployed during landing, with LEV-1 as a relay rover. Pragyan (ISRO Chandrayaan-3, August 2023) rolled out of the lander according to news coverage. Lunokhod 1 is recognised by Guinness World Records as the first lunar or planetary rover (secondary source). The CADRE concept is planned for IM-3.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any specific lander or rover is asserted. The CADRE mission identifies IM-3 as its lander (JPL), but verified interface evidence for stowage, release, mounting and power/data was not retrieved. Compatibility should be assessed against mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, deployment method, power and communications requirements once verified specifications are available.

article.historical_significance: Lunokhod 1, a Soviet rover, is recognised by Guinness World Records as the first lunar or planetary rover (secondary source; secondary sources give about 756 kg and a 2.2 m by 2.2 m footprint). The Japanese and Indian rovers are more recent flown examples. The CADRE concept is an example of a planned cooperative team of small rovers. Demonstrations such as these show that mobility, autonomy and cooperation can be tested on the Moon at small scale.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The SORA-Q mass is 228 g according to JAXA, but secondary coverage gives 250 g; this article uses the JAXA value. The SORA-Q operating duration (about 100 minutes) comes from secondary coverage and is not verified against a JAXA primary source. The Science Robotics paper on SORA-Q was identified in search results but its URL and content were not verified in this run. The Pragyan mass (26 kg) and power (50 W) come from an ISRO brochure excerpt; the brochure URL returned HTTP 404 during this run, and the values are not verified against the primary document. Dimensions conflict across sources and are not stated as verified. No camera or instrument specification was verified for Pragyan. The CADRE mission status and launch date as of the article date were not verified; JPL's page lists the mission as future. CADRE's rover mass, power and dimensions are not published in the source. The ESA LRM is a ground testbed specification and does not represent a flight design. The Lunokhod mass figures (756 kg and 840 kg) conflict across secondary sources. Other rover mobility programmes, including MoonRanger from Carnegie Mellon University scheduled for a 2029 lunar mission, were identified but not described in detail; no mass or dimension was verified for MoonRanger in this run. Crewed lunar rovers (such as the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle) were not researched in this run and are not described here. Any compatibility claim with a specific lander or rover is not made, because verified interface evidence was not available.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Reference URLs were checked for the absence of query strings and fragments. The Pragyan brochure URL contains an encoded space in its path (%20), which is a path component and is retained.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue match: ID 273, name 'Rover mobility demonstrator' and category 14 'Robotics, mobility and deployment technology' confirmed against lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.

The payload name describes a class of technology demonstrations. The article covers four examples (SORA-Q/LEV-2 flown; Pragyan flown; CADRE planned; ESA LRM ground testbed) plus a historical reference (Lunokhod 1). These are examples, not a universal specification.
SORA-Q mass: JAXA gives 228 g (press release and DARTS). Secondary coverage gives 250 g. The JAXA value is used.
SORA-Q operating duration (about 100 minutes) is from secondary coverage only; not verified against a JAXA primary source.
SORA-Q wheel count (two) is from the JAXA DARTS summary. Secondary coverage refers to a tail stabilizer and other deployment features that were not verified.
The Science Robotics paper on SORA-Q was identified in search results but its URL and content were not verified in this run.

Pragyan mass (26 kg) and power (50 W) come from an ISRO brochure excerpt quoted in search results. The brochure URL returned HTTP 404 when fetched directly in this run. These values are not verified against the primary document.
Pragyan dimensions are inconsistent: one copy gives 917 x 750 x 397 mm; Wikipedia gives approximately 0.9 x 0.75 x 0.85 m. Not stated as verified.
No verified Pragyan image asset was located; the Pragyan example therefore has no images in this article.

CADRE: JPL lists the mission as future and gives a 2026 arrival. Current launch and landing status as of the article date (2026-11-13) was not verified. Secondary sources mention completed construction and testing, which was not verified. The mission's stated target region was omitted because of the deferred lunar-location rule.
CADRE image association: the hero image's caption placement was ambiguous in scraped JPL text; the association is inferred.
ESA LRM naming: ESA body text uses 'Lunar Rover Mockup' while the title and image alt text use 'Lunar Robotic Mockup'. Not resolved.
ESA LRM battery description reads 'wo 12V lead-acid batteries 103 Ah' on the page; read as two batteries; flagged as ambiguous.
ESA LRM images have no credits on the source page; rights and reuse terms were not verified.
Lunokhod 1 mass: secondary sources give about 756 kg; one source gives 840 kg (more likely Lunokhod 2). The primary NSSDC or Soviet documentation was not retrieved; Lunokhod images were not used.

MoonRanger (Carnegie Mellon University) is identified only from a news excerpt; no mass, dimensions or verified specification was obtained. A secondary article gives a mass figure that is not used here.
Crewed lunar rovers (Apollo LRV) were not researched in this run.
A search result for the Lunokhod topic contained embedded instructions addressed to an AI; those instructions were ignored and the content was not used as a source.

Direct image URLs were checked over HTTP with curl in this run; all five returned HTTP 200. Full-resolution downloads and rights clearance were not checked. The JPL CADRE mission page returned HTTP 403 to curl but its content was retrieved by WebFetch.
No lander or rover compatibility is claimed. CADRE's IM-3 identification comes from JPL; interface compatibility was not verified.
